samples.summary: CLI OAuth `state` is not bound to the browser that started the flow, so an attacker who can bind a loopback port on the victim's machine can capture the victim's authorization code
samples.evidence:
The change adds a browser binding for the web flow (a `w.`-prefixed state whose other half is the `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, github-auth.guard.ts:128-139, checked at auth.controller.ts:174-188) but the CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:105-111) mints a bare store-backed token with no cookie and no per-browser binding, and auth.controller.ts:190-194 accepts it from ANY browser.

Vector: (1) the attacker binds 127.0.0.1:P on a shared host / container / multi-user dev box the victim also uses; (2) the attacker calls `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=P&nonce=N&code_challenge=C` themselves and reads `state=S` straight out of their own 302 `Location` header — the endpoint is unauthenticated, so S is free; (3) the attacker phishes the victim with `https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=…&state=S`; the victim (already having authorized the app) is silently redirected to `/auth/github/callback?code=<victim's GitHub code>&state=S`; (4) `verifyCallbackState` finds S in the CLI store and returns it, `findOrCreateUser` resolves to the **victim**, and auth.controller.ts:140-149 redirects the victim's browser to `http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=<code>&state=N` — the attacker's listener; (5) the attacker redeems the code at `POST /auth/cli/exchange` with the verifier V they chose in step 2 and receives the victim's access + refresh tokens.

The nonce echo does not help (the attacker picked N) and PKCE does not help (the attacker picked C and holds V). The `state` echo protects the CLI *from* injected codes; nothing protects the *server* from a CLI state replayed in an unrelated browser. The natural fix is to give the CLI state the same cookie half the web state now gets (or to require the CLI's own confirmation of the browser that started it).
searchedFor: grep for consumeState / createState call sites
grep for setAuthCookies / createTokens call sites

samples.summary: The authorization URL carrying both login bindings (nonce + PKCE challenge) is printed to stderr on browser-open failure, which is exactly the headless/agent case; an observer of that log can hijack the pending login
samples.evidence:
`console.error(oauthUrl)` at login.ts:80 emits `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<challenge>`. The comment at login.ts:52-59 and docs/design/cli.md acknowledge that anyone who reads this URL can start their own login under the same nonce and challenge and push the resulting code at the port — and because the victim's CLI holds the matching verifier, it will happily redeem the attacker's code (cli-auth.store.ts:127-132 accepts it: the challenge matches). Result: the terminal is logged into the attacker's account and every subsequent `wafflebase` write lands in the attacker's workspace.

The mitigation chosen (print only when `open` fails) inverts against the CLI's stated audience: headless CI and agent harnesses are precisely where `open` fails and where stderr is captured verbatim into logs and issue reports. The window is the 5-minute state TTL. A binding that survives disclosure of the start URL — e.g. printing only a short user_code and having the CLI hold a secret it never puts on the URL (RFC 8628 device flow), or deriving the nonce from a value the CLI never transmits — would close it.

samples.summary: `/auth` access-log redaction is case- and normalization-sensitive while Express routing is not, so login secrets can still land in the access log
samples.evidence: `logSafeUrl` gates on `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/.test(path)` (app.module.ts:39), an exact, lowercase, literal prefix test on the raw `req.url`. Express's router defaults to `case sensitive routing: false`, so `GET /AUTH/github?mode=cli&nonce=…&code_challenge=…` and `GET /Auth/github/callback?code=…&state=…` are routed to `AuthController` exactly as the lowercase forms are, but neither matches the redaction regex — the full query string (the CLI's nonce and challenge outbound, GitHub's `code` and `state` inbound) is written verbatim to the access log, and the comment itself notes every 4xx on these routes logs at `warn`. Matching against the resolved route (or lowercasing / normalising `path` before the test) closes it. Impact if triggered is precisely the exposure the redaction was added to prevent — a replayable login parked in the log.
searchedFor: read packages/backend/src/main.ts for setGlobalPrefix / router options
grep for 'case sensitive' / router configuration in backend

samples.summary: The server still accepts CLI logins with no nonce and no code_challenge, leaving RFC 8252 §8.9 code injection fully open for any client that does not opt in
samples.evidence: Both bindings are optional server-side: `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` (github-auth.guard.ts:108) yields `undefined` when absent, the controller then emits no `state` echo (auth.controller.ts:144-146), and `consumeCode` returns the userId for an unchallenged code presented bare (cli-auth.store.ts:122-123). Any CLI that does not send the parameters — including the previously shipped one, which by the docs' own compatibility statement must keep working — is redeemed with the exact pre-change semantics: an attacker who guesses the loopback port pushes `http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=<attacker's code>` and the old CLI exchanges it, logging the terminal into the attacker's account. The guard's own bounds are also asymmetric: a malformed `code_challenge` is a 400 (line 101-103) but a malformed/over-long `nonce` is silently dropped (line 108), producing an unbound login the client believes is bound. Consider making both mandatory for `mode=cli` (or gating the legacy path behind an explicit opt-in) once the CLI version floor allows it, and treating a present-but-malformed `nonce` the same way as a malformed challenge.
searchedFor: read docs/design/cli.md compatibility section in the diff

samples.summary: `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and carries no per-route throttle, so an attacker can grow the in-memory CLI state map with attacker-controlled nonce/challenge payloads
samples.evidence: `createState` (cli-auth.store.ts:42-60) inserts an entry held for 5 minutes on every `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<valid>` request. The route has no `@Throttle` decorator (auth.controller.ts:94-95) — unlike `/auth/github/callback`, `/auth/refresh` and `/auth/cli/exchange`, which all pin 10/60s — so it rides the global 120/60s/IP bucket only, and each entry now carries up to 128 bytes of attacker-chosen `nonce` plus 128 of `code_challenge` on top of the token. `cleanup()` only sweeps expired entries, so a distributed or long-lived flood grows the map unboundedly within each 5-minute window. Adding `@Throttle` to the start route (and/or capping the map size) bounds it.

samples.summary: The browser-flow double-submit cookie is unsigned and unbound, so a cookie-tossing sibling subdomain defeats the new CSRF check
samples.evidence: `startWebState` sets `wafflebase_oauth_state` to a raw random value (github-auth.guard.ts:129-137) and `verifyCallbackState` accepts any callback whose `state` equals the cookie (auth.controller.ts:182). Cookies ignore port and are writable by any sibling host on the registrable domain, so an attacker controlling `*.example.com` (subdomain takeover, a stale CNAME, an XSS on a sibling app) can plant a known value in the victim's browser, complete GitHub consent for their own account with the matching `state`, and still land the victim's browser with session cookies for the attacker's account — the forced-login CSRF this control was added to close. `secure` is also only set when `NODE_ENV === 'production'` (line 133), so on a non-production HTTP deployment the value is observable on the wire. Signing the cookie (HMAC over the value with the JWT secret) or using a `__Host-` prefixed cookie would harden it.

samples.summary: `StateEntry.csrf` is minted per login but never read or verified — a dead security control that reads as coverage
samples.evidence: `createState` generates a 32-byte `csrf` (cli-auth.store.ts:48) and `consumeState` returns it (line 78), but no caller anywhere reads it — `auth.controller.ts:190-194` uses only `mode`, `port`, `nonce` and `codeChallenge`. The change touched every other field of this struct and left `csrf` as-is. docs/design/rest-api.md's risk table now acknowledges it in a parenthetical, but a named `csrf` value that nothing validates is a standing invitation for a future reader to assume CSRF is handled here; deleting it (or wiring it into the CLI round-trip) removes the ambiguity.
searchedFor: read consumeState/createState callers in auth.controller.ts and github-auth.guard.ts

verdict.reason: The CLI branch of GitHubAuthGuard (github-auth.guard.ts:85-113) mints a store-backed state and sets no cookie; startWebState (128-139) — the only place OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE is written — is skipped because req.__oauthState is already set (line 115). verifyCallbackState accepts a non-`w.`-prefixed state on mere presence in CliAuthStore (auth.controller.ts:190-201), with no binding to the browser that started the flow; CliAuthStore.StateEntry (cli-auth.store.ts:4-21) carries no browser/session identifier and its `csrf` field has no reader anywhere in the repo. Greps for every `res.cookie(`/`.cookie(` in packages/backend/src show only the two session cookies and the web-state cookie, and GitHubAuthGuard has a single call site (auth.controller.ts:95), so no alternate path supplies the missing binding. The repo's own docs (rest-api.md:394 vs :395, and the active todo's out-of-scope list) describe exactly this asymmetry as accepted, not fixed. Result: an attacker can obtain a CLI state from the unauthenticated start endpoint, phish the victim into GitHub's authorize URL with it, and have the victim's authorization code redirected to 127.0.0.1:<attacker port> (auth.controller.ts:140-149), then redeem it at POST /auth/cli/exchange with the verifier it chose — PKCE and the nonce echo give no protection since the attacker picked both. Precondition is a co-located attacker able to bind a loopback port on the victim's host; impact is full access/refresh token issuance for the victim's account, i.e. critical in the auth/crypto lane. No counterexample found.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. app.module.ts:39 gates redaction on a case-sensitive literal-prefix regex over the raw req.url path, and app.module.ts:87 applies it as the only scrubbing of the URL in the pino req serializer (redact.paths at :95-102 covers headers only). The protected routes really live at /auth/... (auth.controller.ts:43 @Controller('auth'), :94 @Get('github'), :110 @Get('github/callback')) with no global prefix set in main.ts, and they do carry the secrets the comment names (state at :116, nonce/codeChallenge at :140-149). A repo-wide grep for 'case sensitive routing' / 'strict routing' returns no Express router configuration anywhere in packages/, so the framework default of case-insensitive routing stands: an /AUTH/github/callback?code=...&state=... request reaches AuthController but fails the redaction regex, and 4xx on those routes logs at warn (app.module.ts:66-68). Nothing upstream normalizes or lowercases the path, so no already-guarded ground exists, and logged login secrets fall squarely inside the Security lens's secrets / sensitive-data-exposure bullet. The only counter-argument I could build is reduced likelihood (GitHub redirects to a fixed statically-configured callback URL and the CLI emits lowercase paths, so a mixed-case request largely carries the requester's own secrets) - that is an exploitability caveat, not a named refutation ground, so the finding stands.

verdict.reason: Every cited location reads as the reviewer describes. github-auth.guard.ts:85-110 requires only `mode=cli` plus a valid `port`; `nonce` (line 108) and `code_challenge` (line 89-94) are both optional, and only a present-but-malformed challenge is rejected (line 101-103) while a missing or over-long nonce is silently dropped. auth.controller.ts:144-146 then emits no `state` echo, and cli-auth.store.ts:122-123 returns the userId for an unchallenged code presented bare at the unauthenticated POST /auth/cli/exchange (auth.controller.ts:221-228). I grepped the backend for any client-version floor or other server-side gate on this path and found none, so the unbound legacy flow is fully reachable. The in-repo CLI does send both bindings and rejects a stateless callback (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:45-63, 279-284), but that is a client-side guard on one client and does not make the server path unreachable — a previously shipped CLI, which the compatibility statement keeps working, is still exchangeable via an attacker-pushed code at the guessable loopback port (RFC 8252 section 8.9), logging the terminal into the attacker's account. In-lane (auth binding / code injection), real, and not refutable on any named ground.

finding.summary: Browser (non-CLI) GitHub login still sends no OAuth `state`, so the callback validates nothing — forced-login CSRF
finding.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` only mints a state token when `mode === 'cli'` (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:59), and `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` only sets `opts.state` when `req.__cliStateToken` is present (github.strategy.ts:59-62). passport-oauth2 with no `state` option installs a NullStore, whose `verify` always succeeds, so a plain browser login sends no `state` to GitHub and `githubAuthCallback` reaches the web branch with `stateToken === undefined` (auth.controller.ts:119,145) and sets `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` cookies unconditionally. Attack: attacker starts the GitHub consent dance himself, captures the unredeemed `?code=…` from his own callback URL, and gets the victim to load `https://<backend>/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>` (image/iframe/link). The victim's browser is issued cookies for the ATTACKER's account, and everything the victim then creates lands in the attacker's workspace. This diff's own `rest-api.md` risk table records the gap as "Not mitigated" and defers it, and the CLI hardening does not close it — reporting it so the deferral is an explicit decision rather than an implicit one. Pre-existing, not introduced here.

verdict.reason: The claimed gap does not exist in this working tree; the reviewer's cited symbols are from an older revision. GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate falls through to startWebState() for any non-CLI login (github-auth.guard.ts:115-117), which mints a 32-byte random value, stores it in the httpOnly SameSite=Lax `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie scoped to /auth with a 5-minute lifetime, and returns it `w.`-prefixed (github-auth.guard.ts:128-139). GitHubStrategy.authenticate forwards `req.__oauthState` — not `req.__cliStateToken`, which appears nowhere in source, only in prior review artifacts — into `opts.state` (github.strategy.ts:61-67), so passport-oauth2's NullStore is not used for browser logins. On the callback, verifyCallbackState runs before any user lookup or cookie issuance (auth.controller.ts:120); a `w.`-prefixed state is compared against the cookie with the constant-time secretEquals and throws UnauthorizedException on mismatch or missing cookie (auth.controller.ts:174-188), and a callback carrying no state at all hits the terminal UnauthorizedException (auth.controller.ts:203-205). The described forced-login CSRF (victim loads /auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code> with no state) is therefore rejected before setAuthCookies at line 154 is reached; specs at auth.controller.spec.ts:349/367/378 assert these refusals.

finding.summary: The nonce and the PKCE challenge travel in one URL that the CLI prints to stderr and the backend logs on any 4xx — an observer of that single line defeats both "independent" bindings
finding.evidence: `login` builds `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<S256>` (login.ts:53-56) and prints it verbatim with `console.error('Opening browser: ' + oauthUrl)` (login.ts:57) — stderr an agent harness captures into logs, issue reports and shared transcripts. Backend-side, `customLogLevel` in app.module.ts:50 returns `warn` for any `statusCode >= 400`, and the `req` serializer logs the full `req.url` (app.module.ts:69) with no redaction of query params (redact covers only authorization/cookie/set-cookie, app.module.ts:77-84), so the new `BadRequestException('Invalid code_challenge')` path (github-auth.guard.ts:76) writes port+nonce+challenge to the production access log. An attacker who reads that one line inside the 30-second listen window replays the SAME nonce and the SAME `code_challenge` in his own `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>&nonce=<victim nonce>&code_challenge=<victim challenge>` request, consents as himself, and pushes the resulting redirect at `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=ATTACKER&state=<victim nonce>`. The state echo matches, and `consumeCode` accepts because SHA256(victim verifier) equals the reused challenge (cli-auth.store.ts:127-130) — the victim's terminal is logged into the attacker's account. Both bindings derive from values shipped together in one observable string, so the independence claimed in docs/design/cli.md and rest-api.md does not hold against an observer of the authorization request. Mitigations worth considering: do not print the query string (print only a shortened/opaque handle, or a URL without `nonce`/`code_challenge` when a browser can be opened), and/or bind the code to the requesting session so a second authorization request reusing a live nonce is rejected.

verdict.reason: Both halves of the claimed disclosure chain are absent from this repository as described. (1) The CLI does not print the OAuth URL on the normal path: login.ts:64 emits only the literal 'Opening browser for GitHub login...' with no URL; the claimed console.error('Opening browser: ' + oauthUrl) at login.ts:57 does not exist. The single print of oauthUrl (login.ts:80) is gated by 'if (!opened)' at login.ts:75 - reached only when open() throws and the URL is the sole way to continue - and is preceded by an explicit secret warning (login.ts:76-79). That gating is the exact mitigation the finding recommends. (2) The backend does not log the auth query string: app.module.ts:87 serializes url via logSafeUrl(req.url), and logSafeUrl (app.module.ts:34-40) replaces the entire query with '?<redacted>' for any path matching the /auth prefix regex. So the BadRequestException path (github-auth.guard.ts:101-103, not :76) is logged at warn (app.module.ts:68) as /auth/github?<redacted> - port, nonce and code_challenge never reach the access log. I enumerated every other backend consumer of the request URL (app.module.ts:58,70,71 comparison/regex only, never emitted; main.ts:52 path-prefix routing) and none writes the query string. consumeCode (cli-auth.store.ts:114-133) behaves as described, but the replay it enables requires possession of the victim's challenge, which neither verified sink discloses. The residual fallback print at login.ts:80 is a materially narrower, deliberately-guarded case and standard loopback-OAuth practice, not the unconditional leak claimed.
